name: Adin
title: Ancestor of an Israelite clan that returned from exile
summary: Adin is known as the ancestor of one of the many Israelite families that returned from Babylon to Judah following the Persian Empire's policy of liberation. His name appears in the central lists of returning families: Ezra’s register mentions 454 descendants who returned with Zerubbabel, while Nehemiah’s parallel list counts 655—a difference reflecting the complex history behind these records. In a later wave of return, an additional 50 men came under the leadership of Ebed, son of Jonathan. The significance of this family in the restored community is confirmed by the fact that a representative from Adin’s house was among those who sealed the solemn covenant under Nehemiah—a commitment to live according to God’s torah, keep the Sabbath, and preserve the integrity of the community. Through these sources, Adin’s lineage emerges as a concrete example of how genealogical belonging formed the very foundation of Jewish identity and rights in the post-exilic period.

keyEvents.title: Descendants of Adin in Zerubbabel's caravan
keyEvents.description: 454 descendants of Adin returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel during the first return after the Babylonian exile.

keyEvents.title: Recorded in Nehemiah's register
keyEvents.description: The clan of Adin is listed with 655 people in Nehemiah's parallel register of those who returned from exile. The difference from Ezra's figure of 454 may be due to different times of registration or variations in manuscript tradition.

keyEvents.title: Further descendants return with Ezra
keyEvents.description: A group of Adin's descendants, led by Ebed son of Jonathan, returned with Ezra during a later return. This group consisted of 50 men.

keyEvents.title: Sealing the covenant
keyEvents.description: A representative of Adin's clan was among the leaders who sealed the covenant with God under Nehemiah's leadership, committing themselves to follow God's law, keep the Sabbath, and live separately from the surrounding nations.

versions.summary: Adin was the ancestor of an Israelite clan that returned from the Babylonian exile to Jerusalem. His descendants are mentioned in both the books of Ezra and Nehemiah as part of those who returned to the promised land. Some of his descendants were also among those who sealed the covenant with God under Nehemiah.
versions.title: Head of an Israelite clan that returned from exile
versions.reason: [major] The number of Adin's descendants in Ezra 2:15 is 454, but this varies among different manuscripts. Some have 454, others have different numbers. 454 is correct in the Masoretic text.; [minor] It is more precise to say that one of Adin's descendants (or someone bearing the name Adin) sealed the covenant, not necessarily the patriarch himself, given the timeframe.; [critical] 1 Esdras is an apocryphal/deuterocanonical book that is not part of the Protestant canon and does not have a bookId in the standard numbering 1–66. The reference incorrectly points to Ezra 2:15 (bookId 15), which is already covered in keyEvents[0]. This event should be removed as it is duplicative and refers to a book outside the canonical biblical canon without a correct reference.; [minor] The role 'leader' is somewhat imprecise. Adin was primarily known as 'head of a clan' or 'patriarch'. It may be helpful to add 'head of a clan' for clarification.; [minor] The summary is good, but it can be clarified that Adin himself most likely was the patriarch who lived before the exile, and that it was his descendants who returned. The title says 'leader', but the summary should reflect this nuance.; [minor] In Ezra 8:6, the leader is mentioned as 'Ebed, son of Jonathan'. This agrees with the Masoretic text. The description is correct.; [minor] Neh 10:16 (verse 17 in some texts) – verse numbering may vary slightly among different traditions. In the Hebrew text this could be 10:17. Worth noting.

versions.summary: Adin was the ancestor of an Israelite clan that returned from the Babylonian exile to Jerusalem. His descendants are mentioned in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah among those who returned to the promised land. In Ezra's register, 454 of his descendants are counted in the first return with Zerubbabel, while Nehemiah's parallel list records 655 people. Later, an additional 50 men returned with Ezra, led by Ebed son of Jonathan. One representative of this clan was also among those who sealed the covenant with God under Nehemiah's leadership, thereby committing themselves to live according to God's law. Adin's family illustrates the broader movement of Israelite families seeking to rebuild community life in Judah after the exile.

versions.reason: [minor] In Nehemiah 10, the verse numbering varies depending on manuscript tradition. Some texts place Adin in verse 16, while others have verse 17. Verse 16 appears to be correct in most Hebrew texts (Neh 10:17 in some numbering systems). This should be verified, but it is left as is for now.; [minor] The summary is thorough and well-phrased, but closely resembles the two previous versions. Since this is the third version and the evaluation must be stricter, the text should be rephrased to offer a fresher perspective and clearly distinguish itself from earlier versions.; [minor] Since Adin's descendants are mentioned as participants in the covenant sealing and return from exile, considering roles such as "exile lineage" or similar could help clarify the historical context, but the current role descriptions are acceptable.

footnotes.text: The name Adin (עָדִין) is Hebrew and likely means 'chosen,' 'delicate,' or 'fond of pleasure.' It can also be interpreted as 'one who lives in prosperity.' The name appears exclusively in post-exilic texts in the Hebrew Bible, suggesting it became more common during the Persian period.

The difference in numbers between Ezra 2:15 (454 people) and Nehemiah 7:20 (655 people) is one of several numerical discrepancies between these parallel lists. Such variations can be explained by records being made at different times, the clan growing through additions or marriages, or differences among various manuscripts. Similar numerical differences occur for other clans in the same lists.

The sealing of the covenant in Nehemiah 10 was a solemn ceremony in which Israelite leaders and heads of families placed their seals on a written document. The commitments included observance of the Mosaic Law, payment of temple taxes, keeping the Sabbath holy, and a prohibition against intermarriage with surrounding nations. This ceremony represented a renewed commitment to the covenant in a post-exilic context where Jewish identity had to be redefined without royal sovereignty.

The genealogical lists in Ezra and Nehemiah served a crucial function in the post-exilic community: they established who had legitimate rights to settle in Judah and participate in temple service. Clan affiliation was the primary marker of identity, and those unable to document their ancestry were excluded from certain rights (see Ezra 2:59–63).

The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay document discovered in Babylon in 1879, confirms the Persian policy of allowing deported peoples to return to their homelands and rebuild their sanctuaries. Although the cylinder does not explicitly mention the Jews, it provides important historical context for the return described in Ezra and Nehemiah, supporting the biblical account of Cyrus's decree (Ezra 1:1–4).

In 1 Esdras (3 Esdras), an apocryphal/deuterocanonical book, there is a parallel list where Adin's clan is also mentioned. This testifies that genealogical traditions were preserved and continued in various literary traditions during the late Persian and Hellenistic periods.
